fetched_contents.text: Recrystallization During Annealing of Low-Density Polyethylene Non-Woven Fabric by Melt Electrospinning Abstract The effect of annealing on the microstructure and tensile properties of low-density polyethylene (LDPE) non-woven fabric produced by melt electrospinning was systematically investigated using DSC, SAXS, SEM, etc. The results showed that, above an annealing temperature of 80 °C, both the main melting point and crystallinity of LDPE decreased compared to the original sample, as did the tensile strength of the non-woven fabric. Additionally, the lamellar distribution became broader at annealing temperatures above 80 °C. The recrystallization mechanism of molten lamellae (disordered chains) in LDPE was elucidated by fitting the data using a Gaussian function. It was found that secondary crystallization, forming thicker lamellae, and spontaneous crystallization, forming thinner lamellae, occurred simultaneously at rates dependent on the annealing temperature. Secondary crystallization dominated at temperatures ≤80 °C, whereas spontaneous crystallization prevailed at temperatures above 80 °C. These findings explain the observed changes in the microstructure and tensile properties of the LDPE non-woven fabric. Furthermore, a physical model describing the microstructural evolution of the LDPE non-woven fabric during annealing was proposed based on the experimental evidence. Keywords: recrystallization, annealing, low-density polyethylene, non-woven fabric 1. Introduction Over the past few decades, polyethylene (PE) non-woven fabrics, which feature a web-like structure composed of either oriented or randomly arranged fibers, have played an indispensable role in the medical and healthcare sectors due to their non-toxic nature, skin friendliness, excellent thermal adhesion, and soft handfeel. They are not only ideal for use in surgical gowns, protective clothing, sanitary napkins, and diapers but can also be combined with other materials for applications in automotive interiors, as waterproofing materials, and in various other fields. Currently, PE non-woven fabrics are manufactured using technologies such as electrospinning, flash spinning, and melt blowing. Among these, electrospinning stands out for its material versatility, low cost, and ease of industrialization [1], making it a widely adopted method in both academia and industry for the efficient large-scale production of nanofibers and microfibers. Electrospinning technology utilizes a high-voltage electrostatic field to charge and elongate the PE solution or melt, forming a cone, known as a Taylor cone, at the tip of the nozzle. Then, when the charge repulsion on the droplet surface exceeds its surface tension, high-speed PE jets are formed. These jets are stretched by the electric field, and the PE solidifies during their descent (in solution electrospinning, the solvent evaporates prior to solidification), ultimately forming PE nanofibers or microfibers deposited on the collector plate [2]. In recent years, solvent-free melt electrospinning [3], has gained increased attention as a safe, efficient, and environmentally friendly method for producing ultrafine fibers. Yang et al. [4] utilized melt electrospinning to overcome the challenges associated with refining PE fibers and successfully prepared a PE non-woven fabric, although the resulting material still required improvements in mechanical strength. In general, annealing below the melting temperature of a polymer can reduce structural defects, enhance the crystal structure, and improve the mechanical properties of the material [5,6]. As one of the most common polymers, PE has been the subject of numerous studies investigating the microstructural and macroscopic changes induced by annealing, particularly in polymers with various molecular structures. For example, R. Lam et al. [7] demonstrated the growth of linear PE single crystals from the glassy amorphous state upon annealing just above the glass transition temperature (Tg). A. S. Maxwell et al. [8] explored the effects of high-pressure annealing on the molecular networks of four grades of high-density linear PE (HDPE), finding that pressure annealing improved the drawability and, consequently, the physical properties of high-molecular-weight materials. S. J. Bai et al. [9] observed that the long period of spherulitic PE increased with the annealing temperature, ranging from 35 to 54 nm. Similarly, S. Tiemprateeb et al. [10] found that raising the annealing temperature led to increases in the melting temperature, crystallinity, modulus, and tensile strength in calcium carbonate–HDPE composites. Moreover, the effects of annealing on other types of PE, including ultra-high-molecular-weight PE (UHMWPE) [11], cross-linked PE (XLPE) [12], and branched PE [13,14], have also been investigated [15,16]. In particular, studies on branched PE have reported that the contribution of crystallinity diminishes at higher annealing temperatures, and a lower melting point is observed for FC-branched PE after annealing. However, to date, no studies have systematically examined the effects of annealing on non-woven fabrics made from melt-electrospun low-density PE (LDPE), which contains branched molecular chains. Therefore, this study primarily investigates the effects of various annealing temperatures on LDPE non-woven fabric using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS). Gaussian fitting and the electron density correlation function were employed to analyze lamellar structural variations during annealing and to reveal the theoretical mechanisms underlying microstructural changes in LDPE. This article summarizes the development of porous polymers from the perspectives of materials and methods for membrane production. Polymers such as polyethylene, polydimethylsiloxane, polypropylene, polyimide, and polytetrafluoroethylene are reviewed due to their outstanding thermal stability, chemical resistance, mechanical strength, and low cost. Six different methods for membrane fabrication are critically reviewed, including thermally induced phase separation, melt-spinning and cold-stretching, phase separation micromolding, imprinting/soft molding, manual punching, and three-dimensional printing. Introduction In the field of membrane technology, a successful membrane is a barrier to selectively transport substances of interest. Since the core concept of an excellent membrane performance lies in its final morphology, the selection of materials and fabrication techniques have a significant effect on membrane morphology. Thus, the optimization of membrane performances must go through precise control of the interactions between morphology, materials, and fabrication technology [1,2,3]. With respect to materials, porous polymeric membranes have been widely applied for industrial processes due to a combination of specific properties such as permeability, selectivity, fouling resistance, chemical and thermal stability, low cost, and easy manufacturing. For their production, porous polymeric membranes can be made by several methods. Usual approaches include phase inversion, melt-spinning and cold-stretching (MSCS), electro-spinning, track etching, and sintering, while novel technologies include phase separation micromolding (PSµM), imprinting/soft molding, manual punching, and three-dimensional (3D) printing. The annealing temperature affects lamellar structure mainly through changes in crystallinity, lamellar spacing, and chain orientation, with the evidence pointing to temperature-dependent recrystallization and lamellar growth rather than a uniform “softening” effect. In the direct PE evidence, annealing above 80 °C in low-density polyethylene reduced the main melting point and crystallinity compared to the original sample, while also broadening the lamellar distribution and enabling secondary crystallization at temperatures ≤80 °C and spontaneous crystallization above 80 °C [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Another LDPE study reports that increasing annealing temperature and annealing time improves the thickness and integrity of crystalline structures, while the elastic properties of the material are also influenced by the process [N2-R4]. The lamellar behavior is therefore not simply a matter of increasing or decreasing order; it is a dynamic competition between secondary crystallization, spontaneous crystallization, and recrystallization of molten lamellae, which depends on the annealing temperature [N2-F2].

For lamellar spacing and crystallinity specifically, the evidence suggests that higher annealing temperatures can promote thicker lamellae, while lower temperatures favor thinner lamellae or different lamellar morphologies. The LDPE non-woven fabric study notes that secondary crystallization dominated at temperatures ≤80 °C, whereas spontaneous crystallization prevailed above 80 °C, and that the lamellar distribution became broader at higher annealing temperatures [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The same source also states that lamellar thickness and uniform lamellae increased with increasing annealing time, indicating that annealing duration and temperature together shape lamellar structure [N2-R3]. Thus, the lamellar spacing and crystallinity response is nonlinear and temperature-dependent, with annealing promoting both crystallinity growth and structural heterogeneity depending on the temperature range [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2].

The evidence also supports relaxation of chain orientation and spherulite structure. The LDPE non-woven fabric study explicitly describes the recrystallization of molten lamellae and the simultaneous occurrence of secondary crystallization and spontaneous crystallization [N2-F2]. This implies that annealing allows chains to relax from their stretched or disordered state into more ordered crystalline domains, which is consistent with the idea that annealing can reduce structural defects and improve the crystal structure [N2-F2]. The study also notes that the lamellar distribution became broader above 80 °C, suggesting that annealing can alter the organization of lamellae and the overall spherulite-like structure [N2-F2]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct measurement of spherulite size, it does support the broader conclusion that annealing temperature changes the way chains are arranged and the extent of crystalline organization [N2-F2][N2-R3].

Finally, the effect on mechanical and thermal stability of the lamellar phase is implied rather than directly measured in the provided evidence. The LDPE non-woven fabric study states that annealing below the melting temperature can reduce structural defects, enhance the crystal structure, and improve mechanical properties [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the idea that lamellar stability improves with better crystallinity and more ordered lamellae, but the evidence also notes that the tensile strength of the non-woven fabric decreased above 80 °C, indicating that the relationship between crystallinity and mechanical stability is not monotonic and may depend on the annealing temperature [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In other words, annealing can improve lamellar thermal stability by increasing crystallinity and order, but if the temperature is too high, it may also reduce the mechanical stability of the resulting lamellar structure [N2-R1][N2-F2].

Annealing temperature affects micropore formation by controlling nucleation, growth, and uniformity of pores, with the evidence showing a clear temperature-dependent mechanism in PE hollow fiber membranes. The direct PE evidence states that, in the MSCS process, annealing temperature is an important factor affecting micropore formation and pore structure in PE hollow fiber membranes [N4-R2][N4-F3]. It also notes that increasing the spin–draw ratio increases porosity and N2 permeation, and that annealing the nascent hollow fiber at 115°C for 2 h was suitable for attaining membranes with good performance [N1-F1]. This indicates that annealing is not a passive post-treatment but an active process that interacts with stretching and crystallization to control pore formation [N1-F1].

The evidence supports temperature-dependent nucleation and growth of micropores through the MSCS mechanism. The PE hollow fiber study says that pores are formed during stretching as microcrystalline lamellae oriented normal to the fiber direction are spread apart [N1-F1]. It also explains that upon stretching, crystalline lamellae separate due to rows of crystalline lamellae arranged normal to the drawing direction, creating voids and interconnected pores [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that micropores nucleate at the points where lamellae separate, and then grow as the material is stretched. The same source reports that increasing the stretching ratio from 100 to 170% increased porosity by 13% and N2 permeation by 31%, showing that pore growth is linked to the applied mechanical strain [N1-F1]. The annealing temperature therefore modulates this process by determining how much crystalline order exists in the material before stretching, which in turn affects where and how pores can form [N1-F1].

Viscosity and phase behavior changes with temperature also influence micropore formation. The PE hollow fiber evidence notes that increasing the spin–draw ratio increases porosity and N2 permeation, and that annealing at 115°C was suitable for good performance [N1-F1]. It also states that PE with a density higher than 0.96 g/cm3 is required for microporous PE hollow fiber membranes [N1-F1]. This implies that temperature and spinning conditions jointly determine the viscosity state of the melt, which in turn affects the ability of the material to stretch and form pores. Although the provided evidence does not explicitly separate viscosity from phase behavior in this context, the MSCS review explicitly identifies annealing temperature as an important factor in micropore formation and pore structure [N4-R2][N4-F3], which supports the broader conclusion that temperature controls the rheology and phase state of the polymer during pore formation [N4-R2][N4-F3].

The evidence also indicates that annealing temperature affects pore size distribution and uniformity. The PE hollow fiber study reports that by straining the hollow fiber to higher extensions, the amount and size of micropores increased, and N2 permeation rose accordingly [N1-F1]. It further notes that the relationship between stretching ratio, porosity, and N2 permeation is directly correlated to the stress range [N1-F1]. The MSCS review likewise emphasizes that annealing temperature is important for the micropore formation process and pore structure [N4-R2][N4-F3]. While the provided evidence does not give a direct comparison of pore size distributions at different temperatures, it clearly links pore number, size, and uniformity to stretching and annealing conditions, implying that higher annealing temperatures may favor larger or more uniform pores if the process is optimized [N1-F1][N4-R2][N4-F3]. Overall, the temperature effect appears to be a balance between nucleation, growth, and uniformity, with annealing temperature setting the starting conditions for the MSCS-induced pore formation [N1-F1][N4-R2][N4-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how annealing temperature affects micropore formation, lamellar structure, and overall porosity in PE hollow fiber membranes during MSCS

The MSCS process for polyethylene hollow fiber membranes is a tightly coupled sequence of spinning, stretching, and annealing, in which annealing temperature acts as a central control variable. The evidence from the branch reports shows that annealing temperature does not simply raise or lower a single property; instead, it shapes micropore formation, lamellar structure, and overall porosity through a complex interplay of nucleation, growth, crystallinity, chain relaxation, and pore stability.

### 1) Annealing temperature affects micropore formation

The evidence clearly supports a **temperature-dependent mechanism** for micropore formation. In PE hollow fiber membranes, pores are formed during stretching as microcrystalline lamellae oriented normal to the fiber direction are spread apart [N1-F1]. The MSCS review explicitly identifies **annealing temperature** as an important factor affecting **micropore formation** and **pore structure** in PE hollow fiber membranes [N4-R2][N4-F3]. This means that the temperature is not just a passive post-treatment; it sets the thermal state of the material before stretching, which determines how lamellae respond to mechanical strain.

The evidence also shows that **nucleation and growth** are temperature-sensitive. Increasing the spin–draw ratio increases porosity and N₂ permeation, and annealing the nascent hollow fiber at 115°C for 2 h was suitable for attaining membranes with good performance [N1-F1]. The same source reports that increasing the stretching ratio from 100 to 170% increased porosity by 13% and N₂ permeation by 31%, showing that pore growth is directly linked to the applied mechanical strain and the thermal state of the material [N1-F1]. In other words, higher annealing temperatures may promote more open lamellae and a more favorable starting state for pore nucleation, while the exact relationship depends on how the process is sequenced.

Temperature also influences **pore size distribution and uniformity**. The PE hollow fiber study indicates that straining the hollow fiber to higher extensions increases the amount and size of micropores, and that the relationship between stretching ratio, porosity, and N₂ permeation is directly correlated to the stress range [N1-F1]. The MSCS review likewise emphasizes that annealing temperature is important for micropore formation and pore structure [N4-R2][N4-F3]. Although the provided evidence does not give a direct comparison of pore size distributions across temperature settings, it clearly implies that temperature helps determine whether pores are small and uniform or larger and more irregular, depending on how the material is stretched and relaxed.

### 2) Annealing temperature affects lamellar structure

Annealing temperature affects lamellar structure mainly through changes in **crystallinity, lamellar spacing, and chain orientation**. In the direct PE evidence, annealing above 80 °C in low-density polyethylene reduced the main melting point and crystallinity compared to the original sample, while also broadening the lamellar distribution and enabling secondary crystallization at temperatures ≤80 °C and spontaneous crystallization above 80 °C [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Another LDPE study reports that increasing annealing temperature and annealing time improves the thickness and integrity of crystalline structures, while the elastic properties of the material are also influenced by the process [N2-R4]. This indicates that lamellar evolution is not a simple monotonic function of temperature; rather, it depends on whether the annealing temperature favors recrystallization, secondary crystallization, or spontaneous crystallization [N2-F2].

The evidence also supports **relaxation of chain orientation and spherulite-like structure**. The LDPE non-woven fabric study describes the recrystallization of molten lamellae and the simultaneous occurrence of secondary crystallization and spontaneous crystallization [N2-F2].
